items.prompt: In negotiation, what does BATNA stand for?

options.label: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement
Basic Agreement Terms Not Yet Accepted
Balanced Allocation of Terms and Needs Agreed
Best Approach To Navigating Arguments

rubric: BATNA is the best alternative to a negotiated agreement.
Other options are invented expansions of the acronym.

items.prompt: What is a reservation point (walk-away point) in a negotiation?

options.label: The deadline by which the deal must be signed
The midpoint between both parties' opening offers
The first offer a party puts on the table
The worst deal a party would still accept

rubric: The reservation point is the worst acceptable outcome.
Distractors confuse it with the opening offer, midpoint or deadline.

items.prompt: What term describes the overlap between two parties' reservation points, where a deal is possible?

options.label: Concession made to move the other side
Anchor set by the first offer
Zone of possible agreement
Impasse after talks break down

rubric: ZOPA is the range where both parties can accept a deal.
Anchor is the first number, concession is a give, impasse is a deadlock.

items.prompt: In principled negotiation, what should you focus on instead of fixed positions?

options.label: Deadlines
The other side's personality
Opening numbers
Interests

rubric: Principled negotiation separates interests from positions and focuses on interests.
Other options are tactical elements, not the core focus.

items.prompt: What is an anchor in a negotiation?

options.label: A written summary of the terms both sides have agreed
A neutral third party who helps both sides settle disputes
A final offer that one side states cannot be changed
The first offer, which sets the reference point

rubric: An anchor is the first offer that frames the bargaining.
Distractors describe an ultimatum, a mediator and a contract.

items.prompt: Which of the following are steps normally included in preparing for a negotiation? Select all that apply.

options.label: Setting your reservation point
Working out your BATNA
Hiding your interests even from yourself
Deciding to make no concessions whatever
Identifying your interests

rubric: Preparation covers interests, alternatives and limits.
The others are not standard preparation steps.

items.prompt: A buyer and a supplier are discussing a bulk order. The buyer says, 'I want the price at 50 dollars per unit.' In negotiation terminology, what is this statement?

options.label: A BATNA
A mediation request
An underlying interest
A position

rubric: A stated demand or number is a position.
An interest would be the reason behind it, such as budget limits.

items.prompt: Why is a strong BATNA useful in a negotiation?

options.label: It lets you skip setting a bargaining range, since the alternative decides
It guarantees the other party will accept your first offer if it is fair
It forces the other side to reveal their limit once they learn of it
It shows when to walk away and gives you confidence to hold out

rubric: A BATNA is the benchmark for judging offers and supports bargaining power.
Distractors credit it with powers it lacks.

items.prompt: Two sisters both want the same orange. One needs the peel for baking and the other wants the juice. What does this show?

options.label: Opposed positions may hide compatible interests
Concealing your needs gets the best outcome
Splitting the item in half is always the fairest deal
The sister with the stronger claim should win it all

rubric: Different interests behind the same position allow both to gain.
Splitting misses the value-creating solution.

items.prompt: Which best describes a win-win (integrative) negotiation?

options.label: One side concedes now and is repaid in a later deal
Both sides look for options that create extra value for each
Both sides compromise by splitting every issue exactly down the middle
The side with the better BATNA decides the outcome of the deal

rubric: Integrative bargaining expands value through trade-offs.
Splitting down the middle is distributive compromise.

items.prompt: A job candidate's lowest acceptable salary is 60,000 and the employer's highest is 55,000. What is the likely outcome?

options.label: They will settle near 57,500, since both sides split the gap
The candidate's walk-away point must be wrong, since real offers always fall inside it
The employer's maximum will rise to match, since firms always stretch a budget to hire
No zone of agreement exists, so salary alone cannot close a deal

rubric: No overlap means no ZOPA on salary alone.
Midpoint deals need an overlap; other issues might change it.

items.prompt: Why is a very aggressive first offer sometimes risky?

options.label: It signals you will not need to make any concessions later
It reveals your BATNA to the other side right away
It lets the other side set the anchor with a counteroffer
It can seem insulting and make them walk away

rubric: Extreme anchors can damage trust and end talks.
Other options misstate how anchoring works.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why agreements reached through understanding interests tend to hold up? Select all that apply.

options.label: Clear, specific terms leave less room for later disputes
Parties who helped shape terms feel more committed to them
Pressure used to force agreement makes it more lasting
Both sides' real needs are met, so they have less reason to back out
Vague wording lets each side keep their own interpretation

rubric: Met needs, ownership and clarity support durable deals.
Pressure and vagueness tend to cause breakdowns.

items.prompt: A manager and an employee disagree over a request for a raise. The employee says, 'I need 10 percent.' The manager asks, 'What is behind that figure?' and learns the employee mainly wants recognition and growth. What is the manager doing?

options.label: Moving from positions to interests to find more options
Anchoring low to pull the employee's expectations down
Using a strong BATNA to pressure the employee to accept
Making a concession on price to build goodwill early

rubric: Asking why uncovers interests that open more options.
The other choices describe different tactics.

items.prompt: In a negotiation, what is an 'interest'?

options.label: The specific demand a party states aloud as its opening request at the table
The lowest outcome a party would accept before it ends the talks entirely
The amount of money a party hopes to gain from reaching any agreement
The underlying need or concern that explains why a party wants something

rubric: An interest is the need or concern behind a demand; the demand itself is a position.
Distractors confuse interests with positions, walk-away points or money goals.

items.prompt: Why does a strong BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) increase a negotiator's bargaining power?

options.label: Because it obliges the other side to match your best outside alternative exactly
Because it lets you refuse any deal that is worse than your best outside option
Because it hides your interests so that the other side cannot make any proposals
Because it fixes the final price before talks so no further bargaining is needed

rubric: A good alternative means you can walk away from a poor deal, so you are not forced to accept it.
Distractors treat the BATNA as something that binds the other side or replaces bargaining.

items.prompt: What is the zone of possible agreement (ZOPA) in a negotiation?

options.label: The set of issues both sides agree to leave off the agenda for later
The gap between the first offers each side makes in the opening round, which the bargaining then narrows
The price a neutral mediator proposes after both sides reach a deadlock
The range between both sides' walk-away points where a deal benefits both

rubric: The ZOPA is the overlap between the sides' reservation points where both gain from a deal.
Distractors confuse it with opening offers, agenda items or a mediator's proposal.

items.prompt: Why might a well-informed negotiator choose to make the first offer?

options.label: Making the first offer reveals the other side's reservation point right away
Early numbers anchor the discussion, since later offers tend to adjust from that point
Whoever offers first is always seen as weaker, which prompts larger concessions
The first offer legally binds both sides to stay within a fixed range afterwards

rubric: The first number often anchors the talks, so informed negotiators may set it.
Distractors invent binding effects or wrongly claim the first offer exposes the other side's limit.

items.prompt: Why can trading across several issues create more value than splitting a single issue down the middle?

options.label: Issues are bundled so that neither side has to reveal what it really cares about
Each side gives up what it values less in return for what it values more
Both sides end up conceding equal amounts on every issue they discuss
The total money available is fixed and simply gets divided in a fairer way

rubric: Sides value issues differently, so trades let each gain on what matters most to it.
Distractors treat negotiation as a fixed pie or as equal concessions.

items.prompt: Which of the following statements express interests rather than positions? Select all that apply.

options.label: I need a predictable monthly income to cover my rent.
I want room to grow into a senior role within two years.
I will not accept anything less than 5,000 a month.
I care about being able to collect my children by 5 pm.
You must give me the corner office with the window.

rubric: Interests state needs or concerns: income security, growth and family time.
The fixed salary figure and the office demand are positions, not the reasons behind them.

items.prompt: A supplier will sell a machine for no less than 50,000. A buyer can pay at most 60,000 and opens the talks with an offer of 45,000. What does this situation tell you about the negotiation?

options.label: The buyer's maximum must fall to 50,000 before the two sides can reach any agreement at all
The bargaining range runs from 45,000 to 60,000, so any price within it suits both sides
A deal is possible between 50,000 and 60,000, though the opening offer lies outside it
No deal is possible because the buyer's opening offer is below the seller's minimum price

rubric: The overlap of 50,000 to 60,000 is the ZOPA; an opening offer outside it does not remove the possible deal.
Distractors confuse an opening offer with a reservation point.

items.prompt: A seller's lowest acceptable price is 80,000 and the buyer's highest is 95,000. If they settle at the midpoint of the bargaining range, what price results?
rubric: The midpoint of 80,000 and 95,000 is 87,500.
15,000 is the width of the range, not a price.

items.prompt: You are offered a job at 70,000. You hold another written offer at 78,000. Which reply best uses your alternative?

options.label: Say you need 90,000 and will walk away unless they match it immediately today
Keep your other offer secret and ask for time without giving any number or reason
Thank them, mention the competing 78,000 offer and ask whether they can move closer to it
Accept 70,000 now and plan to ask for a raise once you have settled in the role

rubric: Citing a real alternative politely gives a concrete, credible reason to improve the offer.
Distractors give up leverage, issue an unsupported ultimatum or conceal the alternative.

items.prompt: A supplier says, 'That is our final price,' but you need the total cost to be lower. Which next step best applies interest-based negotiation?

options.label: Ask what is driving the price and propose changes to terms such as volume or payment timing
Propose splitting the difference between your last offer and their price right away, to show flexibility and close
Restate your target number more firmly and explain that you have other suppliers who would match it
Accept the price for now and ask for a discount on the next order once the relationship is established

rubric: Exploring the supplier's interests and other terms can lower total cost without a fight over the price.
Distractors rely on pressure, an immediate split or giving in.

items.prompt: You are buying supplies. Your best alternative is a rival supplier at 100 per unit, all costs included. Which walk-away price is most sensible for you?

options.label: Up to 90 per unit
Up to 120 per unit
Up to 80 per unit
Up to 100 per unit

rubric: Your walk-away point should be about your best alternative: pay no more than 100.
Paying 120 is worse than your alternative; 80 or 90 are targets, not limits.

items.prompt: A seller opens at 200 for an item that three market quotes put at about 120. Which response best applies sound negotiation practice?

options.label: Counter at 160 to meet halfway between their price and the market quotes
Offer 50 so that the eventual compromise lands near the figure you want
Accept 200 for now and plan to negotiate fees and extras afterwards instead
Counter near 120 and cite the market quotes as the reason for your number

rubric: Countering with an objective standard resists the extreme anchor and keeps credibility.
Splitting rewards the inflated anchor; an unsupported lowball damages trust.

items.prompt: A client and a contractor disagree about a delivery deadline. Which actions apply principled negotiation? Select all that apply.

options.label: Threaten to cancel the contract so the client backs down quickly.
Insist on the original date as a position that cannot be discussed.
Agree on an objective standard, such as typical timelines for similar projects.
Brainstorm options such as phased delivery before choosing one.
Ask the client why that particular date matters so much to them.

rubric: Principled negotiation explores interests, uses objective criteria and generates options before deciding.
Rigid positions and threats work against it.

items.prompt: You manage a team negotiating with a vendor. Your team cares most about fast delivery, while the vendor cares most about a long contract. Price, delivery speed and contract length are all open. Which package best uses these different priorities?

options.label: Offer a three-year contract in return for guaranteed fast delivery and a modest discount
Trade away fast delivery to win a lower price and keep the contract short
Propose moving each of the three issues exactly halfway between the two positions
Hold to a one-year contract and ask for fast delivery, a discount and extra support

rubric: Trading contract length, which the vendor values, for delivery speed, which you value, creates value for both.
Distractors ignore the differing priorities or split every issue evenly.

items.prompt: You are preparing to buy 200 laptops for your company. Another supplier has already quoted you 900 per unit, delivered. Before the meeting with your preferred supplier, what should you do with this quote?

options.label: Treat it as your BATNA, and set your walk-away point so you would accept their deal only if it beats it
Keep it secret and open with it as your target price so the supplier sees you as firm
Use it as the supplier's reservation value, since it shows what they must charge
Set it aside until the supplier makes a final offer, since alternatives distract from interests

rubric: The competing quote is your best alternative to a negotiated agreement, and it sets your walk-away point.
Treating it as the target price or the other side's reservation value confuses whose limit it represents.

items.prompt: You will pay at most 50,000 for a used delivery van and would like to pay 42,000. The seller's listing is 55,000, and you estimate they would accept 45,000. Which is the bargaining zone (ZOPA)?
rubric: The zone runs from the seller's lowest acceptable price to the buyer's highest acceptable price.
Using targets or the listing price instead of reservation points gives the wrong range.

items.prompt: A colleague wants the shared meeting room every Monday morning; you also want it every Monday morning. Using an interest-based approach, which step should you take next?

options.label: Offer to give up the room now so that your colleague owes you a favour later
Ask why Monday morning matters to each of you, then seek options meeting those needs
Cite the team's room policy and the booking rules to show your claim is more legitimate than theirs
Propose splitting the difference by alternating Mondays, since compromise is the fastest fix

rubric: Exploring the interests behind positions may reveal options that satisfy both sides.
Splitting, citing rules, or conceding skip the step of uncovering interests.

items.prompt: You are negotiating a salary and have researched that comparable roles pay 70,000 to 80,000. You want to anchor the discussion. Which opening is most consistent with that research?

options.label: Ask for 100,000 so that any compromise lands above the market range
Ask the employer to name a figure first, then match it
Ask for 70,000 so that you are seen as reasonable
Ask for 82,000 and explain it using the market data and your skills

rubric: An ambitious but defensible anchor near the top of the supported range is credible and favourable.
An anchor far outside the data damages credibility, and opening at the bottom gives value away.

items.prompt: A vendor says: 'We can only do 10 percent off, and that is our final offer.' You still need a lower total cost. Which response applies the standard technique of expanding the options?

options.label: Restate your original price firmly and wait for the vendor to give way on the limit
Ask the vendor's manager to override the discount, since a higher authority can waive limits
Threaten to walk away unless they match your original number, so they see you have a credible alternative
Accept the 10 percent but ask for free delivery, longer payment terms or a warranty

rubric: Trading on other terms adds value without forcing the vendor to cut price further.
The other options repeat positions or escalate rather than create new options.

items.prompt: You are planning a negotiation to renew a supplier contract. Which preparation steps follow sound practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Set your walk-away point and target before the meeting
Rank your interests and note which ones are tradeable
Estimate your own and the supplier's alternatives
Avoid researching the supplier so you stay open-minded
Plan to reveal your walk-away point early to build trust

rubric: Alternatives, ranked interests and set limits are core preparation.
Revealing the walk-away point early forfeits leverage, and skipping research leaves you unprepared.

items.prompt: You manage a project and ask a client to extend a deadline by two weeks. The client refuses, saying the date is fixed. You know the client's real concern is having the reporting module ready for a board meeting in week 6, while the deadline falls in week 4. What should you do next?

options.label: Split delivery: the reporting module by week 4, the rest two weeks later
Offer a 10% discount on the whole project in return for the two-week extension
Restate that the extension is needed and walk the client through the technical reasons for the delay
Accept the original deadline for all features and warn the client in writing that quality may suffer

rubric: Matching delivery to the client's underlying interest solves the problem without a trade on price.
The other options stay at the position level or concede without exploring needs.

items.prompt: A buyer says 'your price is too high' three times, but never names a figure or a competitor. Which analysis best explains how to proceed?

options.label: Price is probably the true interest here, so offer a discount now and see whether the objection stops
The repeated objection signals a final position, so close at the current price before they walk away
The objection may mask other concerns such as risk or timing, so ask what they compare against
The buyer is likely bluffing to extract a concession, so hold firm and let silence do the work

rubric: A repeated vague objection often hides interests that questions can reveal.
Assuming bluffing or price-only motives skips the diagnosis.

items.prompt: After a two-hour negotiation, both sides agreed on a delivery plan. Three weeks later it collapsed because the operations team that must carry it out was never consulted. Which flaw in the process is the root cause?

options.label: The agreement was reached without the people who must implement it
The opening anchor was set too high, so the final terms were unrealistic for both sides
The parties spent too much time on interests and too little time fixing positions
The negotiators relied on too many objective criteria, which left no room for flexibility

rubric: Agreements fail when those who implement them were not involved or did not commit.
The other causes do not explain failure at implementation.

items.prompt: In a negotiation you offered 20 percent more volume for a lower unit price, and the supplier refused even though that is profitable for them. Which is the most plausible cause to investigate?

options.label: Capacity is limited, so extra volume is a risk, not a gain
Any discount sets a precedent that other buyers will cite
The supplier values volume less than you assumed, so a deeper discount would be needed
The supplier is bluffing to test your resolve before accepting

rubric: An offer's value depends on the other party's constraints, so test hidden constraints such as capacity.
The other explanations are unsupported or ignore the specific facts.

items.prompt: Two negotiators trade offers: A opens at 100, B at 60, A moves to 95, B to 62, A to 90, B to 63. Which pattern does this reveal about the process?

options.label: B is signalling real flexibility by conceding slowly, which invites A to match with smaller moves
A concedes much more than B each round, so A is moving alone while B holds firm
A is anchoring effectively by holding near the opening position and making B come to it
Both sides concede at a similar pace each round, indicating a balanced process of give and take

rubric: Unequal concession sizes set a pattern in which one side gives much more than the other.
Describing the moves as balanced or as anchoring misreads the numbers.

items.prompt: You compare two deals: Deal X pays 120,000 now, while Deal Y pays 100,000 now and 30,000 in a year with a 40 percent chance the buyer defaults. What does the comparison show about expected value if default means no payment?

options.label: X and Y are equal, since risk offsets the 30,000
Y is worth 112,000, so X is higher only if risk counts
Y is worth 118,000 in expectation, so X is higher
Y is worth 130,000 in expectation, so Y is better

rubric: Expected value of Y is 100,000 + 0.6 x 30,000 = 118,000, below X.
Ignoring the default probability or miscalculating leads to the wrong comparison.

items.prompt: A deal collapsed after both sides had agreed on price. Which findings would help explain why it did not hold up? Select all that apply.

options.label: The agreement had no steps for handling disputes
Key terms such as delivery dates were left vague
One party agreed only under time pressure and later felt coerced
The price was within the bargaining zone
Both parties had researched their alternatives beforehand

rubric: Coercion, vague terms and no dispute process all weaken durability.
A price in the zone and preparation do not explain failure.

items.prompt: A freelancer negotiates a rate with a startup. The startup says its budget is fixed at 5,000 for the project. The freelancer wants 7,000. The startup also mentions it hopes to find long-term design help once it raises funds. Which analysis points to the most promising path?

options.label: Trade a lower fee now for a retainer or follow-on work, since the budget is fixed but future need is real
Accept 5,000 now and drop the scope discussion, since the startup's fixed budget is its final position
Treat the budget as a bluff and hold at 7,000, since the startup's hope for later help shows it can pay more
Ignore the startup's funding plans, because future work is uncertain and has no bearing on today's price

rubric: The startup's stated future need is a tradeable interest that can bridge the price gap.
Dismissing the information or conceding without trading wastes available value.

items.prompt: A supplier will not sell below 120 per unit. A buyer cannot pay above 110. Both figures are true, and no other issues have been discussed yet. What does the analysis show?

options.label: Splitting the difference at 115 works, since each side gives up the same amount and meets in the middle of the gap
The gap is small, so a firm refusal by either side will make the other concede past its stated limit in the end
No overlap exists on price alone, so a deal needs more issues or a shift in someone's alternatives
The buyer should open at 100, because a lower anchor will pull the final price into the overlap range

rubric: With reservation points that do not overlap, there is no bargaining zone on price alone, so value must be added or alternatives must change.
Distractors treat the gap as a positioning problem that anchoring or splitting can fix.

items.prompt: A seller opens at double the market price with no explanation. The buyer stops engaging and talks stall. Which analysis best explains this?

options.label: The anchor was implausible and unexplained, so it cost the seller credibility instead of shifting expectations
The buyer was bargaining over positions, so any counter to a first offer would have stalled the talks anyway
Anchors only work when the buyer names the first number, so the seller's opening had no real effect on the talks
The seller showed too little flexibility in round one, which signals rigidity more than an unrealistic number

rubric: An anchor outside the plausible range and without justification damages credibility and can end engagement.
Distractors misattribute the stall to who anchors first or to positional bargaining in general.

items.prompt: A tenant asks a landlord for a 10% rent cut and is refused. The landlord adds that two other units are empty and cash flow is tight. Which reading points to the best trade?

options.label: Empty units show weak alternatives for the landlord, so the tenant should restate the 10% demand with more force
Cash flow worries are irrelevant to price, so the tenant should compare rents in other buildings before talking
The landlord's stance is simply fixed, so the tenant should threaten to leave to test whether the refusal is real
The landlord's interest is steady income, so a longer lease or upfront payment could be traded for a lower rate

rubric: The stated worry reveals an underlying interest (reliable income) that can be traded for the tenant's price goal.
Distractors treat the refusal as a fixed position and respond with pressure.

items.prompt: A counterpart claims to have several rival bidders. Which observation most strongly suggests the claim is a bluff?

options.label: They state the claim calmly but decline to say what the competing prices or terms are at this stage
Rivals are never named, the deadline has moved twice, and they keep booking more meetings with you
They reply slowly to emails and ask for a detailed breakdown of your pricing before giving any figures
They insist the deadline is firm and press for a decision this week without explaining the reason why

rubric: Shifting deadlines and continued engagement with you are behaviours inconsistent with a strong alternative.
Distractors are common behaviours in genuine competitive processes and are weak evidence.

items.prompt: In three rounds you moved your price by 10, 5 and 2 points while the other side moved nothing. Which diagnosis fits best?

options.label: Their silence means your price is still above their limit; keep conceding in smaller steps until they respond
Shrinking steps showed you were near your limit, so they will now accept; hold the last number and wait for them
Your opening 10-point move was too large; starting at 5 would have triggered reciprocity and matching moves from them
Unreciprocated concessions signalled spare room and taught them waiting pays; tie each move to a matching move

rubric: Giving without reciprocation teaches the other side that holding out is rewarded.
Distractors misread their silence as acceptance or blame the size of the first step.

items.prompt: Which features of a negotiation suggest there is room for an integrative, value-creating deal? Select all that apply.

options.label: The parties differ in their forecasts, risk tolerance or time preferences
The parties rank the open issues in different orders of importance
Both parties state the same firm target price and have equal bargaining power
Only price is open, and each side values every extra unit of it the same way

items.prompt: After three weeks of talks, a vendor's account manager agreed to deliver on 1 March with a penalty clause, and signed the contract. Production later says it never agreed and ships on 20 March. The buyer wants to know where the negotiation process failed. What most likely went wrong?

options.label: The buyer pressed too many issues at once, so the vendor agreed to dates just to simplify the negotiation
Nobody checked the account manager's authority or production's buy-in before closing, so delivery lacked backing
The penalty clause was too small to motivate, which is a pricing flaw and not a flaw in who sat at the table
The date was first agreed verbally, and verbal commitments stay unenforceable even after a written contract is signed

rubric: The agreement was made without the people who must deliver, so commitment and authority were never verified.
Distractors blame clause size, issue load or verbal origin rather than the missing party.

items.prompt: You want to keep a long-term supplier relationship and avoid being anchored. The supplier opens 40% above market. Which response best meets both criteria?

options.label: Accept their framing for now and bargain down in small steps so the mood stays friendly throughout talks
Say the figure is far from market, share two benchmarks, and put forward your own supported number
Ignore the figure and ask for their best terms again, hoping they lower it themselves without prompting
Counter 40% below market so the midpoint lands near fair value and the gap looks symmetrical to both sides

rubric: Naming the gap, giving objective benchmarks and offering a justified counter resists the anchor while preserving the relationship.
Distractors either mirror the anchor, avoid the issue or let the anchor stand.

items.prompt: You have two weeks before a key supplier negotiation. Your criterion is to strengthen your walk-away position as much as possible. Which use of the time is best?

options.label: Draft a long list of reasons the supplier needs your business so your value is easy to argue
Research the supplier's history and personal style so you can pace concessions to their habits
Obtain a written quote from a qualified second supplier so the alternative is concrete
Rehearse your opening argument until it is polished so you can present with maximum confidence

rubric: A concrete, documented alternative directly improves BATNA and therefore bargaining power.
Distractors improve presentation or information but do not change the walk-away option.

items.prompt: An employer says the role's base band is capped at 100k and offers 95k. You want total value near 105k and a quick path to higher pay. Which plan best fits these criteria?

options.label: Ask for the 100k cap, plus a sign-on bonus and a written six-month review tied to set targets
Insist on 105k base and cite market data, since a cap is usually negotiable if you stay firm
Ask only for extra vacation and flexible hours, since money is capped and more pay asks look greedy
Accept 95k now and raise pay later, since reopening money talks early could harm the relationship

rubric: It works within the cap while adding value through a bonus and a defined route to higher pay.
Distractors ignore the stated constraint, defer the issue or abandon the pay goal.

items.prompt: A buyer and seller of a small firm disagree: the seller forecasts 20% growth, the buyer 5%, and each believes their own forecast. The criteria are to close the deal and avoid later disputes. Which structure is best?

options.label: Fix a high price now and let the buyer rescind if growth ends below 10% within a year after closing, with the seller refunding in full
Price at the average of the two forecasts, so neither side has to admit its view of the future was wrong
Delay signing a year until real growth is known, then set the price at the observed growth figure, with both sides bound to it
A base price plus an earn-out on sales thresholds defined in the contract and verified by audited figures

rubric: A contingent payment turns the forecast disagreement into a measurable term both can accept.
Distractors average away the difference, create rescission risk or abandon closing the deal.

items.prompt: Two firms must agree a two-year service contract with uncertain demand. The criterion is that the agreement should hold up if conditions change. Which draft is best?

options.label: A fixed price and fixed volume with heavy penalties for deviation, so both sides have strong incentives to comply
A short general statement of intent with terms to be worked out as demand becomes clear over the first year
Defined volume metrics, a price adjustment formula, and a staged dispute process before any termination
A very detailed list of every foreseeable event with a separate fee for each, to leave no gaps for either side

rubric: Adjustment mechanisms and a dispute process let the deal absorb change without collapsing.
Distractors are either too rigid, too vague or falsely exhaustive.

items.prompt: Using the criterion that a party should end talks when the deal is worse than its alternatives or its obligations, which are sound reasons to end talks without a deal? Select all that apply.

options.label: The best final offer is below your BATNA once switching costs and risk are counted
The terms would require you to breach a legal or ethical obligation
The other negotiator has been blunt and unfriendly throughout
You have spent weeks preparing and want that effort to count

rubric: An offer below true BATNA or one requiring a breach justifies walking away.
Sunk effort and the counterpart's tone are not criteria about the deal's value.

items.prompt: A vendor offers a deal 5% under your target price and says it expires in 24 hours. Your alternative is only 2% under target and takes three months to arrange. You cannot confirm that the deadline is real, and you want to try improving terms without risking the deal. What is the best move?

options.label: Accept the core terms in principle and ask for one low-cost improvement, ready to sign as offered if refused
Reject the offer and counter at 7% under target, since a deadline like this is probably artificial anyway
Let the deadline pass quietly to test whether the vendor extends, since your alternative is only slightly worse
Sign immediately without comment, since any request for changes risks the deal and the offer beats your BATNA

rubric: It protects a deal that beats your BATNA while testing for a small gain at low risk.
Distractors either gamble the deal on an unverified deadline or forgo the chance to improve terms.

items.prompt: A procurement lead calls her BATNA strong because 'there are plenty of other suppliers.' Which test best judges whether that BATNA gives her real leverage?

options.label: Whether the number of listed suppliers is large enough to show that the overall market is competitive
Whether a named supplier could deliver on known terms in time, once switching costs and risks are counted
Whether the current supplier accepts that other suppliers exist and could plausibly match her current price
Whether she is willing to state firmly, and credibly, that she will walk away unless the current price falls

rubric: A BATNA is leverage only if it is a concrete, executable alternative valued net of costs and risk.
Distractors confuse market size, bold statements or the other side's agreement with an actual alternative.

items.prompt: You hold solid comparable-sales data for a used-equipment sale; the buyer has little. You want the best price and a close this week. Which opening judgment best fits these criteria?

options.label: Open with a midpoint figure to signal fairness, since that shortens the haggling and secures a close this week
Wait for the buyer to name a figure first, because the first number always gives away information to the other side
Share your reservation price early, so the buyer sees nothing to test and agrees to it quickly this week
Make the first offer near your aspiration, backed by the comparables, so the anchor is set on terms you control

rubric: With better information, an ambitious, defensible first offer anchors the range in your favour.
Waiting or opening at a midpoint wastes the information edge; revealing the reservation price gives away surplus.

items.prompt: A manager settles every impasse by splitting the difference between the last two offers. Judged on incentives across repeated negotiations, what is the main flaw in this habit?

options.label: It rewards extreme openings and slow concessions, because the midpoint shifts toward whoever started further out
It can never reach agreement when the last offers are far apart, so talks stall at the very point of impasse
It delays closure, because each side must wait to learn the other's reservation price before it makes a move
It makes both sides concede equal amounts, which is unfair whenever one of them has more power in the deal

rubric: Predictable midpoint splitting teaches counterparts to inflate positions and stall, since that moves the midpoint.
Distractors raise fairness or reservation-price worries that do not address the incentive effect.

items.prompt: A deal was reached with a negotiator whose authority was never confirmed. Both sides call the price fair. Which risk most threatens the agreement holding?

options.label: Your side's later second thoughts about the price, which could prompt a push to reopen the terms
Ambiguous wording on a delivery date, which each side may later read differently and dispute
Missing penalty clauses for late delivery, leaving you little leverage if performance slips
Terms needing sign-off from an absent principal, who may reject them and reopen the price

rubric: Unconfirmed authority means the counterpart's principal can repudiate or reopen the deal, the biggest threat to durability.
The other options are minor, or concern risks that are not live given the stated facts.

items.prompt: You face a buyer whose priorities you cannot read, and you want to learn them without anchoring on a single number. Which approach best meets that criterion?

options.label: Present two or three packages of equal value to you that trade price, term and support differently, then note the buyer's choice
Make one high offer on price alone and watch how quickly the buyer counters, then infer priorities from it
Offer one package and ask the buyer to list what is wrong with it, then revise it step by step in sequence
Ask the buyer to rank all issues before any offers are made, and rely on those answers when you build proposals

rubric: Equivalent simultaneous packages reveal preferences through choice without committing to a single anchor.
Distractors rely on candour, a single-issue anchor, or slow sequential revision, which reveal less.

items.prompt: A colleague says: 'Positions are noise; only interests matter, so skip distributive bargaining.' Which critiques of this claim are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Interests cannot be learned without asking, so an interest-based approach is impossible in practice
Counterparts often conceal interests, so you must test their claims and keep a reserve position
Positions never reveal anything about interests, so they can safely be ignored in every negotiation
Even when interests are aligned, the final split of created value is distributive and still needs bargaining skill
In a one-off single-issue price deal there is little value to create, so distributive tactics matter more

rubric: Value claiming remains after value creation, single-issue deals are mostly distributive, and hidden interests require testing.
The other options overstate: interests can be probed, and positions often give clues.

items.prompt: A new employer gives you a 24-hour exploding offer at 92k. Your preferred firm decides in five days, and you would take it at 100k or more. You want to keep the bird in hand, avoid bluffing and keep the relationship warm. Which response is best?

options.label: Accept now and plan to renegotiate after you have proved your value, since the offer is already acceptable
Say nothing about the deadline and wait quietly for the preferred firm, hoping the offer stays open on its own
Say you hold a 105k offer so they must raise the figure by tomorrow, then settle quietly on whatever they give
Thank them, give a concrete reason you need until Friday, ask for an extension, and stay open to accepting

rubric: Asking honestly for an extension tests whether the deadline is real while protecting the offer and trust.
Bluffing risks credibility, silence risks losing the offer, and accepting then renegotiating gives away leverage.

items.prompt: A buyer forecasts 10% revenue growth for a target; the seller forecasts 25%. They cannot agree on price. Design constraints: bridge the disagreement, use verifiable measures, and keep the buyer from steering the outcome. Which design fits?

options.label: Base price at the buyer's forecast plus a bonus tied to the buyer's own view of how well integration went
Base price at the seller's forecast, with a refund if growth falls short, judged by the buyer's management accounts
Base price at the buyer's forecast plus a payment triggered by audited revenue above a threshold, with sales diversion barred
Price at the midpoint of the forecasts, paid in full at closing, so no later disputes are possible

rubric: A contingent payment on audited results lets each side bet on its forecast, with protection against steering.
The distractors ignore the forecast gap, or put the measure under the buyer's control.

items.prompt: Approval from a union and a regulator are each conditional on the other's. You need both deals, and neither can be allowed to stall the other. Which negotiation plan meets these constraints?

options.label: Negotiate both in parallel but never mention the link between them, to keep each conversation simple and clear
Negotiate with the union first and keep the regulator link hidden, so your position is not weakened in talks
Close fully with the regulator first, so the union faces an accomplished fact and has less room to resist it
Secure in-principle agreement with each, stating that each depends on the other, then close both together

rubric: Conditional, linked in-principle agreements closed together handle mutual dependence without either side stalling.
Sequencing or hiding the link breaks down once the dependency surfaces.

items.prompt: A partnership agreement keeps being disputed because the parties read 'reasonable efforts' differently. Constraints: keep the relationship, do not reopen price, and create clarity. Which fix fits?

options.label: Reopen the full agreement so every term can be renegotiated, with clearer wording on each issue and a fresh price discussion
Add an annex defining efforts as observable actions, with quarterly checkpoints and a joint review before disputes escalate
Replace the clause with a heavy financial penalty for any shortfall, so that ambiguity is deterred by the cost of failure
Keep the wording but add a clause requiring both sides to interpret 'reasonable efforts' in good faith, with mediation if they differ

rubric: Operational definitions plus a review step fix the ambiguity without touching price or souring the relationship.
Penalties, good-faith language and full reopening either strain trust or leave ambiguity or risk unresolved.

items.prompt: A supplier has publicly vowed never to cut its list price. You need roughly 10% lower effective cost and want to keep the supplier's goodwill. Which path meets both constraints?

options.label: Press publicly for a price cut, so the supplier feels scrutiny and gives in to protect its reputation
Treat the vow as a bluff, propose the cut anyway and escalate to senior management if they decline it
Hold the list price fixed and cut effective cost through volume rebates, longer terms or bundled services
Drop the cost goal, since a public vow cannot be worked around by any deal structure you could design

rubric: Restructuring other terms lets the supplier keep its public stance while you get the lower cost.
Public pressure and escalation harden positions; abandoning the goal ignores creative structuring.

items.prompt: A prep plan lists your interests, BATNA, target, reservation price and opening offer. You will negotiate five issues with a long-term partner and want value-creating trades. What is the most important missing element?

options.label: A list of the partner's past concessions on earlier deals, to cite as precedent when you ask them for similar ones again
A prepared script for applying deadline pressure late in the talks, so the partner feels forced to close on your terms
A second, firmer opening offer prepared as a fallback, so you can anchor high again if the first one is rejected outright
Your ranked priorities across the five issues and a hypothesis of the partner's, to find mutually beneficial trades

rubric: Value-creating trades need each side's relative issue priorities so concessions can be swapped where they cost least.
The others add pressure or precedent but not the information needed for trades.

items.prompt: You are designing an agreement that must hold up over a three-year relationship in which conditions will change. Which features belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Defined performance metrics with scheduled review points where both sides can raise problems
A penalty for any deviation, however small, so that nobody is tempted to depart from the terms
An adjustment mechanism tied to named external factors, such as an index, for price changes
A staged dispute ladder, such as manager talks then mediation, before any litigation is allowed
Removal of all contingent terms so that nothing in the agreement can ever be interpreted differently

rubric: Metrics, review points, escalation steps and pre-agreed adjustments let an agreement absorb change.
Blanket penalties and removing contingencies make the agreement brittle rather than durable.

items.prompt: A seller will not accept under 480k headline price and wants security for what is owed. The buyer can pay only 300k at closing but can pay more from future profits, and values 180k paid over three years at about 150k today. Which structure meets every constraint?

options.label: 300k at closing plus 180k in instalments over three years, secured against the business assets, with no interest
480k all at closing, with the buyer funding the gap through short-term loans at high rates of interest
420k at closing with no further payments, so the seller gets certainty even though the headline is lower
300k at closing plus 180k unsecured, paid only if the business reaches profit targets in the next three years

rubric: It reaches the 480k headline, fits the buyer's cash limit and value, and gives the seller security through collateral.
The distractors break the cash limit, the headline minimum, or the security requirement.
